title: Room Tile Calculation
objective: Return integer tile count given room dimension and optional tile size.
description:
Task: Write a function tiles_needed(l, w, s=1) that tells how many square tiles are needed to cover a rectangular room.
• l and w are the length and width of the room
• s is the side length of one square tile (default value is 1)
• If a room side is not an exact multiple of the tile side, the last row or column still needs a whole tile, so round up in each direction
• Return the tile count as an integer

Example: tiles_needed(10, 10, 3) → 16, because 10 / 3 rounds up to 4 tiles in each direction (4 × 4 = 16).
input_format:
Function signature: tiles_needed(l, w, s=1) -> int
Parameters:
• l: room length (positive integer)
• w: room width (positive integer)
• s: tile side length (positive integer, default 1)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 5, 4 means tiles_needed(5, 4)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
output_format: Return an int: the total number of tiles needed.
hint_1: Tiles needed along the length = ceil(l / s), and along the width = ceil(w / s).
hint_2: Round up with integer maths: -(-l // s) or (l + s - 1) // s.
hint_3: Multiply the two counts to get the answer.
reference_solution:
def tiles_needed(l, w, s=1):
    rows = (l + s - 1) // s
    cols = (w + s - 1) // s
    return rows * cols

title: Seconds to Duration String
objective: Return formatted duration string "Xh Ym Zs" from integer seconds.
description:
Task: Write a function format_duration(sec) that converts a number of seconds into hours, minutes and seconds.
• 1 hour = 3600 seconds and 1 minute = 60 seconds
• Return a string in this exact format: "Xh Ym Zs" (for example "1h 1m 1s")
• Always show all three parts, even when a part is 0
• Hours are not limited to 24

Example: format_duration(3661) → "1h 1m 1s". Example: format_duration(100000) → "27h 46m 40s".
input_format:
Function signature: format_duration(sec) -> str
Parameters:
• sec: number of seconds (non-negative integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 3661 means format_duration(3661)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
hint_1: divmod(sec, 3600) gives the hours and the remaining seconds.
hint_2: Use divmod again on the remaining seconds with 60 to get minutes and seconds.
hint_3: Build the string with an f-string: f"{h}h {m}m {s}s".
reference_solution:
def format_duration(sec):
    h, rest = divmod(sec, 3600)
    m, s = divmod(rest, 60)
    return f"{h}h {m}m {s}s"

title: Scope Shadowing Trace
objective: Predict return value when a local function variable shadows a global variable.
description:
Task: A variable created inside a function is local. If it has the same name as a global variable, it shadows (hides) the global one inside the function, and the global value is not changed.

Assume your file starts with these two global variables:
level = 10
bonus = 5

Write a function compute_shadow(x) that follows these rules:
• Create a local variable named level inside the function and set it to x * 2 (this shadows the global level)
• Read the global variable bonus (do not create a local bonus)
• Return the local level plus bonus
• Do not use the global keyword. The global level must stay 10

Example: compute_shadow(4) → 13, because the local level is 8 and bonus is 5.
input_format:
Function signature: compute_shadow(x) -> int
Parameters:
• x: an integer
The module already contains the globals level = 10 and bonus = 5.
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 4 means compute_shadow(4)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
hint_1: Assigning to a name inside a function makes that name local to the function.
hint_2: Reading a name that is not assigned inside the function uses the global one.
hint_3: So level = x * 2 is local, while bonus is read from the global scope.
reference_solution:
level = 10
bonus = 5

def compute_shadow(x):
    level = x * 2
    return level + bonus

title: Keyword-Only Invoicing
objective: Enforce keyword-only parameters using * syntax to format user billing strings.
description:
Task: In Python, every parameter written after a bare * in the parameter list is keyword-only: the caller must pass it by name.

Write a function format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18) that builds a billing line.
• c is the customer name (a normal parameter)
• amt is the bill amount and must be passed by keyword, for example amt=1000
• rate is the tax rate (default 0.18) and must also be passed by keyword
• tax = amt x rate, and total = amt + tax
• Return exactly: Invoice for <c>: amount=<amt>, tax=<tax>, total=<total>, with each of the three numbers written with 2 decimal places
• If the caller passes amt without its keyword, as in format_inv('Asha', 1000), Python raises TypeError by itself. This is the expected behaviour

Example: format_inv('Asha', amt=1000) → "Invoice for Asha: amount=1000.00, tax=180.00, total=1180.00".
input_format:
Function signature: format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18) -> str
Parameters:
• c: customer name (string)
• amt: bill amount, keyword-only (non-negative number)
• rate: tax rate, keyword-only (default 0.18)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 'Asha', amt=1000 means format_inv('Asha', amt=1000)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
output_format: Return a str in the format: Invoice for <c>: amount=<amt>, tax=<tax>, total=<total>. If a call breaks the keyword-only rule, it raises TypeError (the expected output line is TypeError).
hint_1: A bare * in the parameter list makes every parameter after it keyword-only.
hint_3: You do not need to write any code to raise the TypeError. Python does it for you.
reference_solution:
def format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18):
    tax = amt * rate
    total = amt + tax
    return f"Invoice for {c}: amount={amt:.2f}, tax={tax:.2f}, total={total:.2f}"

title: Loan EMI Computation
objective: Compute monthly loan repayment using standard EMI formula.
description:
Task: EMI (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed amount you pay every month to repay a loan. Write a function calc_emi(p, r, n) that returns the EMI.
• p is the loan amount, r is the annual interest rate in percent, n is the number of months
• Monthly rate: R = r / 12 / 100
• Formula: EMI = p x R x (1 + R)^n / ((1 + R)^n - 1)
• Special case: if r is 0 there is no interest, so EMI = p / n
• Return the EMI rounded to 2 decimal places

Example: calc_emi(100000, 10, 12) → 8791.59.
input_format:
Function signature: calc_emi(p, r, n) -> float
Parameters:
• p: loan amount (positive number)
• r: annual interest rate in percent (non-negative number)
• n: number of months (positive integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 100000, 10, 12 means calc_emi(100000, 10, 12)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
output_format: Return a float: the monthly EMI rounded to 2 decimal places.
hint_1: Compute the monthly rate once: R = r / 12 / 100.
hint_2: Store (1 + R) ** n in a variable because it is used twice in the formula.
hint_3: Handle r == 0 first so you never divide by zero.

title: GCD and LCM Tuple Return
objective: Return a tuple (gcd, lcm) for two integers using Euclidean algorithm.

Task: Write a function gcd_lcm(a, b) that returns both the GCD and the LCM of two positive integers as a tuple (gcd, lcm).
• GCD (greatest common divisor) is the largest number that divides both a and b
• Find the GCD with the Euclidean algorithm: while b is not 0, replace (a, b) by (b, a % b). When b becomes 0, the answer is a
• LCM (least common multiple) = original a x original b // gcd
• Do not use math.gcd
• Return the two values in this order: (gcd, lcm)

Example: gcd_lcm(12, 18) → (6, 36).

output_format: Return a tuple of two ints: (gcd, lcm).

hint_2: Euclid loop: while b: a, b = b, a % b. The GCD is the final a.

title: Quadratic Equation Solver
objective: Return real roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 as sorted tuple, or empty if complex.
description:
Task: Write a function solve_quad(a, b, c) that returns the real roots of the equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 as a tuple. The value of a is never 0.
• Discriminant: D = b^2 - 4ac
• If D < 0, there are no real roots: return an empty tuple ()
• If D == 0, there is one root: return a tuple with one value, (root,)
• If D > 0, there are two roots: return (smaller, larger)
• Roots are x = (-b +/- sqrt(D)) / (2a)
• Round every root to 4 decimal places

Examples: solve_quad(1, -3, 2) → (1.0, 2.0), solve_quad(1, 2, 1) → (-1.0,), solve_quad(1, 0, 1) → ().
input_format:
Function signature: solve_quad(a, b, c) -> tuple
Parameters:
• a: coefficient of x^2 (non-zero integer)
• b: coefficient of x (integer)
• c: constant term (integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1, -3, 2 means solve_quad(1, -3, 2)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
output_format: Return a tuple of floats: () or (root,) or (smaller, larger).

title: Bisection Root Finder
objective: Approximate square root of float N to 6 decimals using binary bisection.
description:
Task: Bisection finds a square root by repeatedly cutting a search interval in half. Write a function sqrt_bisect(n, eps=1e-6) that approximates the square root of n without using math.sqrt() or **0.5. Follow these steps exactly, so that everyone gets the same answer.

Step 1: If n < 0, raise ValueError.
Step 2: Set low = 0.0 and high = max(1.0, n). (When n is between 0 and 1, its square root is larger than n, so high must be at least 1.)
Step 3: While high - low > eps, repeat:
• mid = (low + high) / 2
• If mid * mid < n, the root is in the upper half, so set low = mid
• Otherwise the root is in the lower half, so set high = mid
Step 4: Return round((low + high) / 2, 6).

Examples:
• sqrt_bisect(25) → 5.0
• sqrt_bisect(2) → 1.414214
• sqrt_bisect(0.25) → 0.5
• sqrt_bisect(2, eps=0.001) → 1.414551 (a larger eps stops earlier and gives a rougher answer)
input_format:
Function signature: sqrt_bisect(n, eps=1e-6) -> float
Parameters:
• n: the number whose square root is needed (non-negative number)
• eps: required accuracy, the loop stops when the interval is not wider than eps (default 1e-6)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 25 means sqrt_bisect(25)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
output_format: Return a float: the approximate square root rounded to 6 decimal places. For a negative n, the call raises ValueError (the expected output line is ValueError).
hint_1: Each loop step halves the interval, so the loop needs only about log2((high - low) / eps) steps.
hint_2: Compare mid * mid with n to decide which half to keep.
hint_3: Follow the steps in the description exactly (including high = max(1.0, n)), then return the rounded midpoint.
